title: All Saints (1 November)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Reformation Day: a church that keeps saying it needs mending. Your line was semper reformanda.

Paul opens a letter to a small church in a Roman town with a greeting that sounds too grand for it: "To all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi." Not just to the leaders. Not to a few heroes. To all the saints. He means the people in the room: a businesswoman who traded in purple, a jailer and his household, some who were quarreling. Ordinary people, meeting in a house, called saints. Later the church would give famous names their own days through the year. And then one day for the rest. Every saint, known and unknown. Today, All Saints.

In the New Testament, saint means holy one, someone set apart for God, and Paul uses it for whole congregations. Over time the church also used the word for particular people whose lives shone, and gave some of them a day. But a calendar has only so many days, and plenty of faithful people left no name anyone remembers. All Saints is for all of them at once. Hebrews gives the picture. After a long list of faithful people from Israel's story, it says: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." Like runners in a stadium, the stands packed with those who've already finished the race. Revelation widens it: John sees "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues," standing before the throne. That's the crowd this day honors. Churches keep it differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor the saints and ask them to pray for them, as you might ask a friend. Protestant churches tend to remember the saints as examples and companions, giving thanks for them without asking for their prayers. In some churches, a hymn sung on this day begins, for all the saints. Here, at least, the churches can meet. And the day doesn't remember only the famous ones in stained glass. It remembers the grandmother who prayed every night, the teacher who stayed late, the neighbor who quietly kept faith. Paul's greeting went to people like them.

Let the faces come of people who showed you, by how they lived, what goodness or faith looks like: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who stayed, someone you met once and never forgot, living or gone. Say their names quietly, one at a time, with a little space after each. If you pray, thank God for each; if you don't, simply give thanks for them, and let the stands fill up.
All Saints. The feast for every saint, known and unknown: the whole cloud of witnesses, a multitude no one could number.
Your line: for all the saints. Known and unknown, the stands are full. That's day one thousand fifty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches keep a feast of all the saints, often singing 'For All the Saints'; Orthodox churches keep their All Saints Sunday after Pentecost rather than in November.

chat.meaning: In the New Testament a saint is a holy one set apart for God, and Paul greets all the saints at Philippi. All Saints is for every one.

Philippi.meaning: a Roman town whose small church got Paul's letter

cloud of witnesses.meaning: Hebrews' picture of the faithful who ran before

multitude.meaning: a huge crowd; Revelation's is too big to count

kindreds.meaning: an old word for families or clans
